headings.title: Introduction to Human Nutrition and Basic Body Needs
headings.content: Human nutrition is a fundamental pillar of health, growth, and disease prevention, especially within the context of clinical nursing in Nigeria. For nursing students, understanding basic body needs involves recognizing how the human body ingests, digests, absorbs, transports, utilizes, and excretes nutrients to maintain physiological homeostasis. Every living cell requires a continuous supply of chemical substances derived from food to fuel metabolic processes, repair damaged tissues, and support immune function. Inadequate intake or poor utilization of these substances leads to malnutrition, which significantly delays recovery, increases hospital stays, and heightens morbidity and mortality rates among vulnerable populations such as infants, pregnant women, and the elderly. Nutritional assessment and support are therefore core competencies for nurses in both community health centers and tertiary hospitals. By grasping the foundational concepts of energy balance, nutrient density, and dietary adequacy, nurses can better educate patients, plan effective therapeutic diets, and identify early warning signs of nutritional deficiencies. Ultimately, optimizing patient nutrition accelerates wound healing, enhances drug efficacy, and promotes overall well-being across the lifespan.

headings.title: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats
headings.content: Macronutrients are the cornerstone of human energy metabolism, required by the body in large quantities daily. They are broadly categorized into carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. Carbohydrates serve as the primary and most efficient source of cellular energy, yielding approximately four kilocalories per gram, and are vital for proper brain function and red blood cell metabolism. They are classified as simple or complex, with complex carbohydrates offering sustained energy and dietary fiber crucial for gastrointestinal motility. Proteins are complex polymers made of amino acids, essential for structural growth, tissue repair, enzyme synthesis, and immune defense; they also provide four kilocalories per gram when utilized for energy. Certain amino acids are termed 'essential' because the human body cannot synthesize them, meaning they must be obtained directly through diet from sources like legumes, fish, eggs, and meat. Fats, or lipids, are concentrated energy sources yielding nine kilocalories per gram while providing insulation, organ protection, and serving as vehicles for fat-soluble vitamins. Nurses must understand the distinct roles of saturated, unsaturated, and trans fats to provide sound dietary counseling, particularly for patients managing cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, or renal disorders.

headings.title: Micronutrients: Essential Vitamins and Minerals
headings.content: Micronutrients, consisting of essential vitamins and minerals, are required by the body in minute quantities yet are absolutely critical for biochemical reactions, fluid balance, bone density, and immune defense. Vitamins are organic compounds divided into water-soluble (such as Vitamin C and the B-complex vitamins) and fat-soluble (such as Vitamins A, D, E, and K). Water-soluble vitamins are easily excreted in urine and require regular daily intake, whereas fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the liver and adipose tissue, posing a risk of toxicity if consumed in excessive amounts. Minerals are inorganic elements further categorized into major minerals (like calcium, phosphorus, sodium, and potassium) and trace minerals (like iron, iodine, zinc, and copper). For instance, iron is indispensable for hemoglobin synthesis and oxygen transport, while calcium is vital for neuromuscular transmission and skeletal integrity. In Nigeria, micronutrient deficiencies such as iron-deficiency anemia, vitamin A deficiency, and iodine disorders remain major public health concerns. Nurses play an active role in identifying deficiency symptoms, administering therapeutic supplements, and educating communities on consuming diverse, nutrient-dense local foods to prevent these conditions.

headings.title: The Role of Water and Hydration in Cellular Function
headings.content: Water is the most abundant and indispensable component of the human body, accounting for roughly 50 to 60 percent of total adult body weight. It serves as the primary medium for all metabolic and cellular reactions, acts as a solvent for nutrients and electrolytes, regulates core body temperature through perspiration, and facilitates the elimination of metabolic wastes via the kidneys and bowel. Cellular function entirely depends on maintaining precise fluid and electrolyte balance across intracellular and extracellular compartments. Dehydration occurs when fluid output exceeds intake, leading to cellular shrinkage, hemoconcentration, impaired renal function, and cardiovascular collapse if severe. Conversely, fluid overload can cause edema, hypertension, and pulmonary congestion, particularly in patients with compromised heart or kidney function. Nurses must meticulously monitor fluid intake and output (I&O), assess skin turgor, evaluate mucous membranes, and recognize early signs of dehydration or fluid retention in patients. In clinical scenarios involving fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or burns, prompt intravenous or oral rehydration therapy is a life-saving nursing intervention that restores hemodynamic stability.

headings.title: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) and Daily Energy Expenditure
headings.content: Energy balance is governed by the relationship between caloric intake and total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). The Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) represents the minimum amount of energy required by the body to maintain basic, life-sustaining functions—such as respiration, circulation, and temperature regulation—while at complete physical, digestive, and emotional rest. BMR accounts for the largest component, roughly 60 to 75 percent, of an individual's daily energy expenditure. Several factors influence BMR, including age, sex, body surface area, thyroid hormone levels, and body composition, with lean muscle mass consuming significantly more energy at rest than adipose tissue. Total daily energy expenditure also includes the thermic effect of food (the energy required to digest, absorb, and metabolize nutrients) and physical activity energy expenditure, which varies widely depending on lifestyle and occupational demands. Nurses must understand energy calculations and metabolic principles to evaluate nutritional requirements accurately, ensuring hospitalized patients receive adequate calories to prevent catabolism, muscle wasting, and delayed wound healing.

headings.title: Physiological Factors Affecting Nutritional Requirements
headings.content: Nutritional requirements are not static; they fluctuate dynamically across the human lifespan and in response to various physiological states. During infancy and childhood, rapid growth and cellular multiplication demand high caloric and protein intake relative to body weight. Adolescence brings a rapid pubertal growth spurt accompanied by increased needs for calcium, iron, and energy. Pregnancy and lactation place uniquely high demands on the female body, requiring increased intake of folic acid to prevent neural tube defects, along with elevated proteins, iron, and calcium to support fetal development and milk production. Conversely, aging adults experience a gradual decline in lean muscle mass and basal metabolic rate, which reduces overall caloric needs, though their need for micronutrients and high-quality protein remains high to prevent sarcopenia and bone fragility. Furthermore, pathological states such as surgery, major trauma, burns, and severe infections trigger a hypermetabolic stress response, breaking down body tissues and exponentially increasing nutritional demands. Nurses must tailor dietary plans by factoring in these unique physiological variables to promote optimal healing and prevent malnutrition.

headings.title: Socioeconomic, Cultural, and Environmental Influences on Diet
headings.content: Dietary habits and nutritional status are heavily shaped by socioeconomic, cultural, and environmental determinants. Socioeconomic status directly affects food security, dictating an individual's or family's purchasing power to access diverse, safe, and nutrient-dense foods. In many regions of Nigeria, poverty limits food choices, often leading to carbohydrate-heavy diets that lack sufficient quality protein and micronutrients. Cultural practices, traditional beliefs, and religious observances also dictate dietary taboos and food preferences; for example, certain communities may restrict pregnant or lactating women from consuming nutritious foods like eggs or specific meats based on cultural myths. Environmental factors, including geographical location, agricultural productivity, climate change, droughts, and food distribution infrastructure, further dictate what foods are locally available and affordable. As patient advocates and educators, nurses must approach nutritional counseling with cultural sensitivity and awareness of these external pressures. Effective nursing interventions must respect local traditions while offering practical, affordable, and culturally acceptable strategies to improve dietary intake and overcome nutritional deficits.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment of Nutritional Status
headings.content: A comprehensive nursing assessment of nutritional status is essential for early identification of malnutrition, guiding timely interventions, and monitoring clinical outcomes. The nursing nutritional assessment follows a systematic approach known by the mnemonic ABCD: Anthropometric measurements, Biochemical data, Clinical examination, and Dietary history. Anthropometric measurements include height, weight, Body Mass Index (BMI), mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC), and skinfold thickness, which help quantify body fat and muscle stores. Biochemical data involve laboratory evaluations such as serum albumin, prealbumin, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and electrolyte panels that reflect visceral protein status and micronutrient levels. Clinical examination entails a physical head-to-toe assessment for visible signs of malnutrition, such as dry brittle hair, pale conjunctiva, angular stomatitis, edema, or muscle wasting. Dietary history evaluates the patient's usual food intake, eating patterns, cultural food preferences, and any swallowing difficulties. By synthesizing these findings, nurses formulate accurate nursing diagnoses related to nutrition and collaborate with dietitians and physicians to implement effective nutritional care plans.
